headline: Jama was originally a Buddhist term, from Middle Chinese 邪魔, literally “wrong, evil, perverse” plus “devil, demon”.

sources.quote: Originally a Buddhist term, imported into Japanese when Buddhism was introduced to Japan, some time during the Kofun, Asuka, and Nara periods.
From Middle Chinese 邪魔 (MC zjae ma, literally “wrong, evil, perverse" + "devil, demon”). Compare modern Mandarin 邪魔 (xiémó).

headline: Yurui appears to be derived from the archaic verb 揺る (yuru, “to shake, sway”).

sources.quote: Appears to be derived from the archaic verb 揺(ゆ)る (yuru, “to shake, sway”).

sources.quote: Cognate with the verb 励む (hagemu).

headline: Yahari may be a hypercorrect back-formation from やっぱり (yappari).

sources.quote: Frellesvig views the pronunciation yahari as a hypercorrect back-formation from やっぱり (yappari), since intervocalic -p- would typically yield -w- and not -h- in modern Japanese. Compare the yapa- root in 柔(やわ)らか (yaparaka → yawaraka, “soft; pliant”), thought to be related. The pronunciation may be due to a spelling pronunciation of やはり, which could ambiguously represent yawari, yafari~yahari, or yappari in older texts. Dictionaries generally consider やはり the older form.
/japari/ → /jaɸari/ → /jahari/
/japari/ → (emphatic) /jappari/ → (back-formation) /jahari/

headline: Ishokujū is 衣 (i, “clothing”), 食 (shoku, “food”) and 住 (jū, “shelter”).

sources.quote: Compound of 衣(い) (i, “clothing”) + 食(しょく) (shoku, “food”) + 住(じゅう) (jū, “shelter”).

headline: Taki, “waterfall”, is simply listed as from Old Japanese.

sources.quote: /taki₁/ → /taki/
From Old Japanese.

headline: Kanarazushimo is 必ず (kanarazu, “certainly”) plus the emphatic しも (shimo), the same one seen in 誰しも (dareshimo).

sources.quote: From 必(かなら)ず (kanarazu, “certainly, (negative polarity) not necessarily”) + しも (shimo, emphatic word). The しも (shimo) can also be seen in 誰しも (dareshimo) and まだしも (madashimo).

headline: Atsumari is the continuative stem of 集まる (atsumaru).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 集(あつ)まる (atsumaru).

headline: Tadashii is 直 (tada, “straight; direct; straightforward”) plus the adjective suffix し, first appearing in 858 CE.

sources.quote: Derived from 直 (tada, “straight; direct; straightforward”) + し (-shi, adjective-forming suffix, origin of and superseded by modern しい (shii)).

First appears in 858 CE in the 大智度論 (Daichido-ron), the Japanese rendering of the Chinese text Da zhidu lun. Used primarily in 漢文訓読 (kanbun kundoku, “Japanese-language readings of Classical Chinese texts”, literally “Chinese text, meaning (Japanese) reading”) contexts, with almost no usage in 和文 (wabun, “Japanese texts”) or kana contexts until after the Heian Period.

headline: Waribiki is the continuative stem of 割り引く (waribiku).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 割(わ)り引(び)く (waribiku).

headline: Kūchū, “sky”, was borrowed from Middle Chinese 空中, glossed “sky; air + middle”.

sources.quote: Borrowing from Middle Chinese 空中 (MC khuwng trjuwng, “sky; air + middle”).

headline: Asatte shifted from asate, and the kanji spelling comes from myōgonichi.

sources.quote: /asate/ → /asat̚te/
Shift from earlier asate (see Etymology 2 below).
The kanji spelling is from myōgonichi (see Etymology 3 below).

headline: Negai is the continuative stem of 願う (negau).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 願(ねが)う (negau).

headline: Akuma is Middle Chinese 惡魔, literally “bad, evil + demon”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 惡魔 (MC 'ak ma, literally “bad, evil + demon”).

headline: Yome has several theories, all reading it as よ (yo) plus 女 (me, “woman, female”); the yo may be 呼 (“to call out, invite”) or 弱 (“weak”).

sources.quote: There are several theories, all of which analyse it as よ (yo) + 女(め) (me, “woman, female”). However, よ (yo) may be one of the following:
* 呼 (“to call out, invite”, in reference to welcoming the daughter-in-law as the son’s wife)
* 弱 (“weak”, in reference to the inferior position relative to the mother-in-law)
* 夜 (“night”, in reference to serving the husband at night)
* 良 (“good”)
* 吉 (“good luck”)
